title: Ephemeral lane reclamation and SLA-backed burst eviction for Dedicated GPU pools
creator: Ava Thompson
description:
Summary:
We need a mechanism that reclaims ephemeral GPU lanes used for short-lived burst traffic while guaranteeing committed throughput for reserved tenants. Current soft-fencing allows noisy bursts to degrade committed SLOs during overlap windows. This ticket designs an SLA-backed ephemeral lane reclamation system that: (1) maintains throughput guarantees for committed lanes, (2) allows transient bursts to use spare capacity, and (3) gracefully evicts or degrades bursts when capacity is required for committed traffic.

Goals:
- Ensure reserved tenants meet contract throughput 99th/95th objectives even under noisy bursts from other tenants.
- Provide bounded, explainable eviction behavior and preemption-notify hooks for burst consumers.
- Integrate with autoscaler so reclaimed capacity triggers proactive autoscale decisions for dedicated pools.
- Emit telemetry for per-tenant reclaimed tokens, eviction causes, and SLO impact for billing/QA.

Design overview:
1) Ephemeral lanes and credit buckets:
- Tenants can consume ephemeral lanes (a.k.a. burst lanes) up to a configurable burst_limit (tokens/sec) backed by a credit bucket. Buckets refill at a baseline rate; unused credits carry over within rolling windows to encourage smoothing.
- Credit consumption is tracked per GPU lane and per-tenant to allow fine-grained reclamation.

2) SLA-backed priority tiers and eviction signals:
- Each tenant has a priority tier: Committed (reservation), BestEffort (ephemeral), and Fallback (lower tier). When aggregate demand approaches capacity, scheduler computes a ReclaimPlan that: (a) identifies BestEffort lanes to reclaim based on least-recently-used, lowest credit bank, and worst SLO delta; (b) attempts gentle degradation first (rate-limit to X%), then full preemptive eviction for the remaining requests.
- Eviction reasons are enumerated: CAPACITY_SHORTFALL, SLO_DEFICIT, HARD_MAINTENANCE, TOPOLOGY_CONSTRAINT. These reasons are surfaced to tenants via preemption webhook and console events.

3) Preemption grace windows and probe-based detection:
- Before hard eviction, we send a PreemptWarning event with a grace window (configurable, default 2s) to the BestEffort consumer. Within the window the consumer can checkpoint or fall back. If consumer does not respond, we escalate to rate-limited execution and then eviction.
- We add a probing loop that proactively samples tail latency and memory pressure on lanes likely to be candidates for preemption; probe results factor into reclaim ranking.

4) Autoscaler integration and predictive reclaim:
- Reclaim events feed a short-term predictive autoscale signal. If repeated reclaim events from capacity_shortfall are observed for a pool and projected demand growth > 15% over 5 minutes, autoscaler issues a scale-up suggestion or an automated burst allocation depending on policy.

5) Safety nets and rollback:
- Two-tier safety net: (i) Soft fallback: automatically convert some ephemeral requests to queued or degraded mode (lower concurrency) before eviction; (ii) Hard safety: preemption cannot evict a Committed tenant. We expose an override flag for emergency operator actions.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: ephemeral_credits_used, reclaim_plan_id, preempt_warning_sent, eviction_count_by_reason, reclaimed_gpu_seconds, autoscale_suggestion_count.
- Dashboards: per-pool reclaim heatmap, per-tenant eviction timeline, SLO regressions tied to reclaim windows.
- Audit events persisted for billing reconciliation when bursts were throttled/evicted.

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit + e2e tests covering reclaim ranking, preempt warning lifecycle, autoscaler signal emission, and non-eviction of Committed tenants.
- Load test: simulate bursty BestEffort traffic mixed with steady Committed tenants; Committed throughput stays within 1-2% of target (95th percentile).
- Console UI shows reclaim events and tenant notifications.
- PRs merged and feature flag gated in prod for one pool.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Short grace windows may still cause failed user requests — we mitigate with warning hooks for client libraries.
- Frequent evictions could oscillate autoscaler behavior; thresholds must be tuned.
- Increased telemetry volume — we limit cardinality to tenant_id, pool_id, reclaim_reason.

Rollout plan:
- Canary 1: Feature flag enabled for internal test pool. Collect metrics and iterate (2 weeks).
- Canary 2: Enable for low-risk customers with non-critical workloads (1 week).
- Gradual ramp: enable by pool and region; monitor SLOs and eviction counts (2-4 weeks).

Links and artifacts:
- Design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/cp/ephemeral-reclaim-design
- Proto + API RFC: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/ephemeral-reclaim-rfc
- Load test dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.com/d/abcd/ephemeral-reclaim-load-test
- Initial PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/9217

Open questions:
- Should we monetize reclaimed-burst overflow differently (discounted billing) or keep existing billing semantics?
- Default grace window: 2s vs 200ms trade-off between user-visible errors and latency SLA for Committed tenants.
- Policy for cross-pool reclamation when topology constraints leave pockets of idle GPUs.

Next steps (short-term):
- Implement reclaim-ranking prototype in scheduler (Ravi).
- Add PreemptWarning event and client-side handler spec (Ava).
- Create telemetry schema and Grafana panels (Observability SRE).
